The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation granted marketing authorisation for the live, attenuated tetravalent vaccine developed by Takeda GmbH, to be imported by Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India Pvt. Ltd. Qdenga targets all four dengue virus serotypes and is given as two 0.5 ml doses three months apart via subcutaneous injection. Approval rests on global clinical data, including a pivotal Phase III India study and studies in Brazil, Thailand and Sri Lanka, with WHO prequalification and regulatory clearance in 42 countries; more than 24 million doses distributed worldwide. Post‑marketing surveillance indicates a favourable safety profile. The vaccine is expected to complement, not replace, vector control, disease surveillance, early diagnosis and case management under the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, with vaccination strengthening overall dengue prevention.

articleHeadline: Monsoon Update: Dengue Surges As India Battles Double Disease Burden; Malaria, Kala-Azar Decline While NCDs Rise
articleSummary: Dengue dominates India’s monsoon vector-borne disease landscape with a surge from July, while malaria declines by about 60% from 2018 (4.30 lakh) to 2022 (1.74 lakh) and kala-azar is nearly eliminated though eastern regions remain affected. National data from NCVBDC and the Health Ministry (National Health Profile 2018–2022) show dengue cases rising from 2018 (1.24 lakh) to 2019 (2.05 lakh), then 2020 (44,585), 2021 (1.93 lakh) and 2022 (1.67 lakh). In 2022, malaria’s burden peaks in West Bengal (40,563), followed by Chhattisgarh (30,028), Odisha (23,770), Jharkhand (19,129) and Maharashtra (15,437). Amid infectious disease pressures, non-communicable diseases—hypertension, diabetes and cancer—emerge as India’s long-term burden, underscoring the need for prevention and early screening.

articleHeadline: Ebola Outbreak in DRC Spreads Rapidly Amid Ongoing Security Challenges
articleSummary: Bundibugyo virus Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has rapidly expanded to more than 2,400 confirmed cases and nearly 1,000 deaths since May. It spans Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo and has crossed into Uganda. There is no approved vaccine or specific treatment for this variant. Transmission is via close contact with infected bodily fluids and contaminated surfaces; symptoms include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, vomiting, diarrhea, and sometimes bleeding. Ongoing security challenges hinder access and care, though some areas report no secondary cases yet. WHO notes the outbreak is moving faster than prior DRC events; risk to other countries remains low, though travel restrictions and quarantines have been implemented. International partners are expanding testing, contact tracing, safe burials, and community engagement, with thousands trained to identify and isolate cases. A humanitarian worker exposed in the DRC was evacuated to London for observation.

articleSummary: India's drug regulator (DCGI) has approved Takeda's Qdenga dengue vaccine for individuals aged 4–60, marking the first dengue vaccine license in the country. Qdenga is a live attenuated, tetravalent vaccine given in two doses three months apart, with no prior dengue infection required. Approval is based on Takeda's global program, including 19 phased trials (over 28,000 participants) and Phase 3 TIDES data from eight dengue-endemic countries showing 80.2% efficacy against lab-confirmed dengue 12 months after the second dose, and a 90.4% reduction in dengue-related hospitalisations at 18 months, with sustained protection across all four serotypes for about 4.5 years. India-specific Phase 3 trials confirmed safety and efficacy. Qdenga has approvals in 43 countries, with over 32 million doses distributed through public and private programs. WHO recommends use in high-transmission areas; Brazil, Argentina, Colombia, and Indonesia include it in national programs. Takeda will coordinate with Indian authorities to ensure accessibility.

articleHeadline: 今年蚊子变多了？注意这八类场景正悄悄"养"出蚊子！ _光明网
articleSummary: Summer mosquito density in 2026 is higher than in prior years in parts of China, with Guangdong reporting elevated vector indices; Beijing’s hot, humid conditions accelerate breeding. Authorities pursue integrated mosquito-borne disease control: source reduction, smart disinfection, public education, and border defenses. Guangdong, Hainan, and Zhejiang mobilize communities to eliminate standing water and maintain breeding-site registries; Hangzhou parks deploy biomimetic smart traps; Guangzhou releases Wolbachia-infected sterile males to suppress populations. The primary dengue and chikungunya vector, Aedes albopictus (flower mosquito), breeds in small, stagnant water, with eggs maturing rapidly. Eight common breeding sites are: home containers (plant pots); garden items (lotus jars, bamboo, leaf litter, tree holes); general containers (mop buckets, lids); discarded rubbish; tarpaulins; drainage channels; public facilities (hollow poles, umbrella bases, tires); and other outdoor debris. Prevention emphasizes draining water, bite avoidance, and early medical care; use EPA-registered repellents (DEET, picaridin, etc.), with careful guidelines for children.

articleSummary: Brazilian actress Isabella Scherer, pregnant with her third child, has been diagnosed with toxoplasmosis. The diagnosis was made at the tenth week of gestation after a positive test; she described crying and feeling desperate. She postponed an abroad trip due to fear. She began treatment promptly and reports that the baby was not affected, likely due to early detection and immediate therapy; she says she caught the infection within the first three days. Toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondii; transmission can occur via undercooked meat, contaminated water or produce, or soil containing infected cat feces. In pregnancy, infection can cause fetal ocular and neurological complications. Precautions include avoiding undercooked meat, washing fruits/vegetables, hand hygiene after handling raw foods, and wearing gloves when gardening. After sharing the diagnosis, she faced criticism and suggested that her father-in-law's cats, Olympic swimmer Fernando Scherer (Xuxa), might have been involved; she defended herself, saying she did not blame felines and criticized misinformation.
